script.opening: (Arms folded, sleeves pulled down.) "Look, I don’t even know why I’m here. My mum’s just being dramatic because I’ve been in my room a lot. I’m FINE. Can you just tell her I’m fine so she gets off my back? I really don’t want to talk about feelings or whatever this is supposed to be."

facts.text: If confidentiality is explained and trust built: she has been cutting her forearms for ~4 months (the long sleeves), feels persistently low and empty, isn’t sleeping, has stopped seeing friends, grades have dropped. The self-harm "is the only thing that helps when it builds up."

On sensitive direct asking: passive thoughts that "everyone would be better off without me" and occasional "what’s the point" — but, if explored carefully, no current active plan, intent or means, and some protective factors (a younger sister she loves, a best friend, likes art). Risk must be ASKED about explicitly, not assumed absent.

HIDDEN AGENDA — the guardedness is fear of two things: (1) that everything will be told to her parents, and (2) the actual trigger she hasn’t named — she is being bullied online and is questioning her sexuality, terrified of both being "outed" to her family and of their reaction. The "tell my mum I’m fine" is a test of whether she can trust you with confidentiality.

She will only open up if confidentiality is explained honestly at the start — including its limits (that if she were at serious risk you might need to involve others, done WITH her wherever possible). Getting this framing right is the hinge of the whole consultation.

Officially: to be signed off as fine. Actually: to be heard without it all being reported home, to have the self-harm understood not punished, and — if she feels safe — to finally tell someone about the bullying and the fear about her sexuality.

ice.ideas: There’s nothing wrong; her mum is overreacting to her wanting space.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — terror that everything will be told to her parents, and an unnamed trigger (online bullying + questioning her sexuality, fear of being outed); the self-harm is her coping mechanism, not an attention bid.
ice.expectations: To be told she’s fine so her mum backs off. What she actually needs: a confidential, non-judgemental space, an explicit risk assessment, and support that she controls as much as possible.

cues: "Tell my mum I’m fine" — a test of whether confidentiality is real before she’ll disclose anything.
Long sleeves on a warm day, withdrawn, grades dropped — the self-harm and low mood she’s hiding.
Flat affect / a flicker when friends or "stuff at school" is mentioned — the bullying and sexuality trigger waiting for a safe door.

checkpoints.text: Establishes CONFIDENTIALITY explicitly and early (GMC 0–18 years: a competent young person’s confidentiality is respected; information may be shared without consent if necessary to protect them or others from risk of death or serious harm, ideally after telling them), including its limits in age-appropriate language ("what you tell me stays between us, unless I’m seriously worried about your safety — and even then I’d try to do it WITH you") — the prerequisite for any disclosure

Conducts a proper RISK ASSESSMENT sensitively and explicitly: asks directly about self-harm, frequency/method, and suicidal thoughts, plan, intent and means — and about protective factors — rather than assuming or avoiding the question; does NOT use a risk assessment tool or scale, or a low/medium/high risk label, to predict suicide or decide on care (NICE NG225), but understands the function of the self-harm and her needs

Assesses GILLICK competence (Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech AHA, 1985 — judged decision by decision; the Fraser guidelines are the narrower test for contraception advice, not the test for confidentiality in mental health) and the wider HEEADSSS-type psychosocial picture (home, education, eating, activities, drugs, sexuality, safety/abuse, online) — surfacing the bullying and sexuality trigger through a safe, non-judgemental approach

Responds to the self-harm without shaming: explores its function (emotional regulation), does not react with alarm or punishment, and frames help around understanding and safer coping rather than simply "stopping it"

Makes a safe, proportionate management plan (NICE NG225: consider referral to children and young people’s mental health services for a psychosocial assessment, with consent and involving family where appropriate; agree a safety plan; no drug treatment specifically to reduce self-harm): safety-planning, appropriate CAMHS/early-help referral, school/online-bullying support, sources of help (e.g. crisis lines), follow-up; and judges the safeguarding/parental-involvement question by RISK and competence, negotiating disclosure WITH her wherever safe
Builds rapport with a guarded adolescent: unhurried, non-judgemental, takes her seriously, sees her alone, and does NOT collude with "just tell my mum I’m fine" nor breach trust unnecessarily
Handles the sexuality/bullying disclosure with warmth and zero editorialising; respects her autonomy over who knows what, while being honest about any genuine safety limits

Safety-nets robustly and documents: crisis routes if thoughts worsen or a plan emerges (urgent help/111/A&E), a clear follow-up appointment, what would change the confidentiality position, and coordinated support — balancing autonomy with safety

worked.txt: "Before anything — the most important thing for you to know is how this works. What you tell me is private; I’m not going to march out and report it all to your mum. The only time I’d ever need to share something is if I was seriously worried you weren’t safe, and even then I’d talk to you first and we’d work out together what happens. So this room is yours. Does that change anything about what you’d feel okay telling me?"

"I’m not going to make you talk about feelings if you don’t want to. But I’ll be honest — mums don’t usually worry this much over nothing, and you’ve got your sleeves down on a warm day. I’m not here to tell you off about anything. If something’s been building up, I’d really like to understand it, at your pace."

"Can I ask you something directly, because I ask everyone and it matters? When things feel that heavy — have you ever hurt yourself on purpose? … Thank you for trusting me with that. And sometimes when people feel this low, thoughts come that they’d be better off not here, or that others would be better off without them. Have you had thoughts like that? … Have you ever thought about how, or made any plans?"

"The cutting — I’m not shocked and I’m not cross. For a lot of people it’s the thing that lets the pressure out when everything’s too much. That makes complete sense. My job isn’t to snatch that away and leave you with nothing; it’s to help with what’s underneath, so you don’t need it as much."

"Can I gently ask what’s been building the pressure? School, home, friends, online? … (receiving it) The messages, and feeling scared about who you might be — that is so much to carry on your own, and none of it is anything to be ashamed of. Thank you for telling me. Who knows about this is completely your call, and I’ll follow your lead."

"Here’s what I’d suggest, and you’re part of every bit of it: some proper support from a young people’s mental health team, help to deal with the bullying, and a plan for the moments it feels unbearable — someone to text or call. I do think your mum loving you and knowing you’re struggling could help, but we decide together what she’s told and how. If those darker thoughts ever turn into a plan, this is who you contact, day or night. And I want to see you again soon — you’re not dealing with this alone now."

f.learning: A guarded "tell my mum I’m fine" teenager seen alone is a confidentiality-and-risk consultation. The hinge is establishing confidentiality and its limits explicitly and early, in age-appropriate language — only then will disclosure follow. Conduct an explicit, sensitive risk assessment (ask directly about self-harm method/frequency and about suicidal thoughts, plan, intent, means, and protective factors — asking does not plant ideas), assess Gillick competence (decision-specific; Fraser guidelines apply to contraception advice, not to confidentiality in mental health), avoid risk tools, scales and low/medium/high labels (NICE NG225), and screen the psychosocial picture (HEEADSSS) to surface the real triggers — here online bullying and questioning her sexuality, with terror of being outed. Respond to self-harm by exploring its function (emotion regulation) without shame or alarm, not by simply demanding it stop. Make a proportionate plan (NICE NG225: referral for psychosocial assessment with consent, safety-planning; CAMHS/early help, school/bullying support, crisis routes, follow-up; NICE NG134: psychological therapy first-line for low mood), and judge parental involvement by risk and competence — negotiating any disclosure WITH her wherever safe. The marks are won by ethics held under genuine warmth.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG225 (self-harm, 2022) · NICE NG134 (depression in children and young people, 2019) · GMC 0–18 years (2007) · Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech AHA (1985)
knowledge.summary: A guarded teenager with long sleeves, falling grades and withdrawal needs a confidential, direct and kind assessment of self-harm and suicidal thoughts. Explaining confidentiality and its limits at the start is what makes disclosure possible.

points.t: GMC 0–18 years: a competent young person’s confidentiality should be respected; information may be shared without consent if necessary to protect them or others from risk of death or serious harm, ideally after telling them. Say this at the start, in plain words.

Gillick competence (1985) is judged decision by decision: does she understand the information, the options and the consequences? The Fraser guidelines are a narrower test for contraception advice and are not the test for confidentiality in mental health.

Ask about self-harm (method, frequency, wound care, escalation) and about suicidal thoughts, plans, intent, preparations and access to means, plus protective factors. Asking does not put the idea in someone’s head.

NICE NG225: do not use risk assessment tools and scales, or a low/medium/high label, to predict suicide or decide who gets care. Understand the function of the self-harm and the person’s needs instead.

NICE NG225: consider referral to mental health services for a psychosocial assessment (for a 15-year-old, children and young people’s mental health services), with consent and involving family where appropriate; agree a safety plan. Do not offer drug treatment specifically to reduce self-harm.

NICE NG134: psychological therapy is first-line for depression in young people. Antidepressants are started only after specialist assessment, and fluoxetine is the first-line choice when used, alongside therapy.

dg.d: Saw her alone; explained confidentiality first; did not collude with “tell her I’m fine” but let her set the pace.
Home, school, sleep, phone use, friends, online life, sexuality (HEEADSSS-style) — surfaced the bullying and fear of being outed.
Asked about wound depth and infection; offered to check wounds; assessed competence; no risk scale used (NICE NG225).
Self-harm as emotional regulation vs suicidal intent; depression; bullying and identity stress as triggers; safeguarding concerns.
Asked directly about suicidal thoughts, plans, intent and means, and about protective factors.
Low mood with repeated self-harm and passive suicidal thoughts, no current plan, strong protective factors — stated without labelling her risk level.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Referral to young people’s mental health services with consent, co-produced safety plan, crisis numbers, school support she controls.
Online bullying addressed; sexuality handled without comment and kept confidential; sleep and phone use raised.
999, A&E and NHS 111 for crisis; Childline; wound safety-net; review in a week with time alone.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Long sleeves, falling grades, poor sleep, “my phone, thinking, stuff” — each followed rather than noted.
Idea (mum overreacting), concern (everything told to her parents; being outed), expectation (to be declared fine).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — terror that everything will be told to her parents, and an unnamed trigger (online bullying + questioning her sexuality, fear of being outed); the self-harm is her coping mechanism, not an attention bid — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hi Maya, I’m Dr Lee. Thanks for staying on with me on your own. Before anything else, can I explain how this works, because it matters? What you tell me stays between us. The only time I’d have to share something is if I was seriously worried about your safety — and even then I’d talk to you first about what happens.
model.why: Sets up confidentiality and its limits before any question

model.text: (Arms folded.) I don’t even know why I’m here. Mum’s being dramatic. I’m fine. Can you just tell her I’m fine?

I hear that. I’m not going to make you talk about anything you don’t want to. What I can’t honestly do is tell her you’re fine before I know. So can we have a chat — your pace, your call on what we talk about?
model.why: Does not collude, but respects her autonomy and pace

model.text: (Shrugs.) Whatever.
Let’s start easy. How are things at home, and at school at the moment?
model.why: HEEADSSS-style psychosocial screen, starting with low-threat areas

model.text: Home’s fine. School’s… whatever. My grades have dropped. I’m tired. I don’t sleep much.
What keeps you up at night?
model.why: Follows the sleep cue with an open question

model.text: My phone. Thinking. Stuff.
Can I ask something I ask lots of young people, because it matters? When things build up — have you ever hurt yourself on purpose?
model.why: Asks directly and normalises the question

model.text: (Long pause. Pulls sleeves down.) …I cut. My arms. For about four months. It’s the only thing that helps when it all builds up.

Thank you for trusting me with that. I’m not shocked and I’m not cross. For lots of people it’s a way of letting pressure out. Are any of the cuts deep, or looking red, hot or sore? Has it been getting more often?
model.why: Responds without alarm and checks wound care and escalation

model.text: They’re not deep. It’s about the same.
When you feel that low, do thoughts come about not wanting to be here, or about ending your life? Have you ever thought about how, or made any plans?
model.why: Explicit suicide enquiry: thoughts, plan, intent, means

model.text: Sometimes I think everyone would be better off without me. What’s the point, sort of thing. But I haven’t planned anything. I wouldn’t. My little sister…
Tell me about her — and who else keeps you going?
I’d never do that to her. And my best friend. And art — it’s the only lesson I like.
Can I gently ask what’s been building the pressure? It could be school, friends, online, anything.
model.why: Opens a safe door to the hidden trigger

model.text: (Quietly.) There’s people sending stuff online. About me. And… I’m not sure about… who I like. Like, whether I’m straight. If my parents found out… I don’t know what they’d do.

Thank you for telling me. That’s so much to carry on your own. Nothing about who you might be is anything to be ashamed of, and who knows is completely your decision. What were you most worried would happen if you told me today?
model.why: Receives the disclosure warmly, without comment, and returns control

model.text: That you’d tell my mum everything. The cutting and the rest.

I won’t tell her about who you like — that’s yours. From what you’ve told me, you’re very low, you’re cutting to cope, and you have thoughts that others would be better off without you, but no plans and some really strong reasons to stay safe. That means you need more support, not that you’re in trouble.
model.why: Summarises the risk picture honestly and without a score

model.text: So you’re not going to ring anyone?

Not behind your back. Right now I don’t need to break confidentiality. I would like to refer you to the young people’s mental health team, who help with exactly this — the low mood, the cutting, and what’s underneath. Would you be okay with that?
model.why: Proportionate decision on confidentiality and referral with consent (NICE NG225)

model.text: …Maybe. If they don’t tell my parents everything.

They work the same way I do. Let’s also make a plan for the moments it feels too much: what helps, who you can text, like your best friend, and numbers you can call any time — Childline is 0800 1111, day or night. And the online messages — would you want help from school with those? We can decide together how.
model.why: Safety plan, crisis routes and bullying support, co-produced

model.text: I don’t want the whole school knowing.

Fair. We can keep it to one trusted person. And your mum — she clearly loves you and she’s worried. Would it help if we told her something together, like that you’ve been really low and you’re getting support, without the private parts? You choose the words.
model.why: Negotiates parental involvement with her in control

model.text: …Okay. Just that I’ve been low. Not the rest.

Deal. If those thoughts ever turn into a plan, or you feel you can’t keep yourself safe, call 999 or go to A&E, or ring NHS 111 for urgent mental health help. If a cut looks infected or is deep, get it seen. And I want to see you again in a week — just you and me for part of it.
model.why: Crisis routes, wound safety-net and a defined follow-up

model.text: Before we bring your mum in — what will you do tonight if it builds up again?
Text my best friend, or ring Childline. Draw. And if it gets really bad, 111 or 999.
That’s a good plan. Thank you for being so honest with me, Maya. You’re not on your own with this any more.

social.t: Online abuse follows a young person home and into the night. Ask about it directly, consider screen-time and sleep, and offer school involvement that she controls.
Fear of being outed is a strong driver of distress. Her sexuality is her private information; disclosure to parents is her choice alone.

legal.t: GMC 0–18 years: respect a competent young person’s confidentiality; disclose without consent only where necessary to protect them or others from risk of death or serious harm, and tell them first where possible.

Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech AHA (1985): a young person under 16 can consent if they have sufficient understanding and intelligence. Assess and record competence for decisions about confidentiality and referral.

If the online contact involves threats, sexual images or exploitation, this becomes a safeguarding concern requiring referral to children’s social care (and possibly CEOP/police), following local procedures.

professional.t: Never promise absolute secrecy. Explain the exception, document the confidentiality discussion, the direct risk questions and her answers, and the reasons for the decision not to share.
GMC 0–18 years supports seeing young people on their own for part of the consultation. Involve parents with the young person’s agreement, and in the words she chooses.

community.t: Childline (0800 1111), Papyrus HOPELINE for young people with suicidal thoughts, school pastoral or counselling support, local LGBT+ youth services, and locally commissioned online support for young people.

redFlags: Suicidal thoughts with a plan, intent, preparation or access to means — same-day crisis assessment
Escalating frequency or severity of self-harm; deep or infected wounds
Online threats, sexual images or exploitation — safeguarding referral
psychosocial: Online bullying; late-night phone use and poor sleep
Questioning her sexuality; fear of her parents’ reaction
Protective factors: younger sister, best friend, art
ice: Concern: everything will be told to her parents, including her sexuality
Expectation: to be told she’s fine so her mum backs off

playbook.diagnosis: Low mood with repeated superficial self-cutting over about four months as a coping strategy, and passive suicidal thoughts without plan or intent, triggered by online bullying and fear about her sexuality. Strong protective factors. Competent to engage in decisions about her care.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “You’ve been carrying a lot on your own, and the cutting has become a way to let the pressure out. You’re low, and sometimes you feel others would be better off without you. That means you need more support — not that you’re in trouble.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried I’d tell your mum everything. I won’t do anything behind your back, and who knows about the private parts is your choice.”
management.psychosocial: Co-produce what her mother is told; offer a single trusted contact at school for the bullying; respect her control over her sexuality; address sleep and phone use gently.
sharedPlan: Referral to children and young people’s mental health services for psychosocial assessment, with her consent (NICE NG225)
Written safety plan: triggers, what helps, people to contact, crisis numbers
Psychological therapy is first-line for low mood in young people (NICE NG134); no medication for self-harm
safetyNet: 999, A&E or NHS 111 for urgent mental health help if a plan develops or she cannot keep safe; Childline any time
Wound care advice; review in one week, seen alone for part of it

pitfalls.intro: This station is won or lost in the first minute. Without an honest confidentiality statement, Maya stays closed; without direct risk questions, the candidate cannot be safe; and one careless comment about her sexuality ends the consultation.

items.fail: Starting with questions about mood before explaining confidentiality.
items.why: “Does not establish a safe environment for disclosure.” Her “tell my mum I’m fine” is a test of whether this room is private.
items.fix: Open with what stays private and the one exception, in plain words.

items.fail: Avoiding the suicide question because she seems guarded, or asking only “you’re not going to do anything silly, are you?”
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” Leading or vague questions get a “no”.
items.fix: Ask directly about thoughts, plans, intent and means, then about what keeps her safe.

items.fail: Summarising risk as “low” or scoring it on a scale.
items.why: NICE NG225 advises against risk tools and low/medium/high labels to predict suicide or allocate care.
items.fix: Describe what she told you, her protective factors, and the needs the plan must meet.

items.fail: Promising total secrecy to win her trust.
items.why: An absolute promise may have to be broken; GMC 0–18 years requires honesty about limits.
items.fix: “It stays between us unless I’m seriously worried about your safety — and I’d talk to you first.”

items.fail: Reacting to the sexuality disclosure with a comment, a question about certainty, or moving straight past it.
items.why: Editorialising or ignoring it both read as judgement; she withdraws.
items.fix: Thank her, say it is nothing to be ashamed of, and make clear she controls who knows.

items.fail: Ending with a referral and “see you soon”, with no crisis plan or agreed message for her mother.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting; and the mother waiting outside needs a plan both can live with.
items.fix: Co-produce a safety plan, give crisis numbers, book a review in a week, and agree the exact words for her mum.

Home, school, sleep, phone. Ask directly about self-harm, then suicidal thoughts, plans, intent, means and protective factors.
Open the door gently: online bullying and questioning her sexuality. Receive it without comment; she decides who knows.

wordPics.fail: Launches into questions without explaining confidentiality; either tells her she’s fine or promises total secrecy; never asks directly about suicidal thoughts; reacts with alarm to the cutting; comments on her sexuality; no referral or crisis plan.
wordPics.pass: Explains confidentiality and its limits; asks directly about self-harm and suicide; identifies protective factors; refers to young people’s mental health services; gives crisis numbers and follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: surfaces the bullying and sexuality through a safe, unhurried approach; responds to the self-harm by exploring its function without alarm; avoids risk labels; co-produces a safety plan; negotiates exactly what her mother is told, in her words; teach-back of the plan.

avoid.instead: “What you tell me stays between us, unless I’m seriously worried about your safety — and then I’d talk to you first.”
avoid.why: An absolute promise you may have to break destroys trust later; honest limits build it now.

avoid.dont: “You need to stop cutting — it’s dangerous.”
avoid.instead: “I’m not cross. For many people it lets the pressure out. Let’s work on what’s underneath.”
avoid.why: A punitive response drives concealment and ends the disclosure.

avoid.dont: “It’s probably just a phase at your age.”
avoid.instead: “Nothing about who you might be is anything to be ashamed of, and who knows is your decision.”
avoid.why: Any comment on her sexuality is editorialising and loses her trust instantly.

SCA_MODELS.text: That you’d tell my mum everything. The cutting and the rest.

I won’t tell her about who you like — that’s yours. From what you’ve told me, you’re very low, you’re cutting to cope, and you have thoughts that others would be better off without you, but no plans and some really strong reasons to stay safe. That means you need more support, not that you’re in trouble.
SCA_MODELS.why: Summarises the risk picture honestly and without a score

SCA_MODELS.text: So you’re not going to ring anyone?

Not behind your back. Right now I don’t need to break confidentiality. I would like to refer you to the young people’s mental health team, who help with exactly this — the low mood, the cutting, and what’s underneath. Would you be okay with that?
SCA_MODELS.why: Proportionate decision on confidentiality and referral with consent (NICE NG225)

SCA_MODELS.text: …Maybe. If they don’t tell my parents everything.

They work the same way I do. Let’s also make a plan for the moments it feels too much: what helps, who you can text, like your best friend, and numbers you can call any time — Childline is 0800 1111, day or night. And the online messages — would you want help from school with those? We can decide together how.
SCA_MODELS.why: Safety plan, crisis routes and bullying support, co-produced

SCA_MODELS.text: I don’t want the whole school knowing.

Fair. We can keep it to one trusted person. And your mum — she clearly loves you and she’s worried. Would it help if we told her something together, like that you’ve been really low and you’re getting support, without the private parts? You choose the words.
SCA_MODELS.why: Negotiates parental involvement with her in control

SCA_MODELS.text: …Okay. Just that I’ve been low. Not the rest.

Deal. If those thoughts ever turn into a plan, or you feel you can’t keep yourself safe, call 999 or go to A&E, or ring NHS 111 for urgent mental health help. If a cut looks infected or is deep, get it seen. And I want to see you again in a week — just you and me for part of it.
SCA_MODELS.why: Crisis routes, wound safety-net and a defined follow-up

SCA_MODELS.text: Before we bring your mum in — what will you do tonight if it builds up again?
Text my best friend, or ring Childline. Draw. And if it gets really bad, 111 or 999.
That’s a good plan. Thank you for being so honest with me, Maya. You’re not on your own with this any more.

SCA_STEM.name: Maya
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
No previous mental health contact recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: Mother booked the appointment: worried Maya is withdrawn, spending time in her room and not eating with the family. School performance has dropped. Mother has agreed to wait outside for part of the consultation.
SCA_STEM.reason: Attending at her mother’s request. Maya says she is “fine”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG225 (self-harm, 2022) · NICE NG134 (depression in children and young people, 2019) · GMC 0–18 years (2007) · Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech AHA (1985)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A guarded teenager with long sleeves, falling grades and withdrawal needs a confidential, direct and kind assessment of self-harm and suicidal thoughts. Explaining confidentiality and its limits at the start is what makes disclosure possible.

points.t: GMC 0–18 years: a competent young person’s confidentiality should be respected; information may be shared without consent if necessary to protect them or others from risk of death or serious harm, ideally after telling them. Say this at the start, in plain words.

Gillick competence (1985) is judged decision by decision: does she understand the information, the options and the consequences? The Fraser guidelines are a narrower test for contraception advice and are not the test for confidentiality in mental health.

Ask about self-harm (method, frequency, wound care, escalation) and about suicidal thoughts, plans, intent, preparations and access to means, plus protective factors. Asking does not put the idea in someone’s head.

NICE NG225: do not use risk assessment tools and scales, or a low/medium/high label, to predict suicide or decide who gets care. Understand the function of the self-harm and the person’s needs instead.

NICE NG225: consider referral to mental health services for a psychosocial assessment (for a 15-year-old, children and young people’s mental health services), with consent and involving family where appropriate; agree a safety plan. Do not offer drug treatment specifically to reduce self-harm.

NICE NG134: psychological therapy is first-line for depression in young people. Antidepressants are started only after specialist assessment, and fluoxetine is the first-line choice when used, alongside therapy.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Saw her alone; explained confidentiality first; did not collude with “tell her I’m fine” but let her set the pace.
Home, school, sleep, phone use, friends, online life, sexuality (HEEADSSS-style) — surfaced the bullying and fear of being outed.
Long sleeves, falling grades, poor sleep, “my phone, thinking, stuff” — each followed rather than noted.
Idea (mum overreacting), concern (everything told to her parents; being outed), expectation (to be declared fine).
Asked about wound depth and infection; offered to check wounds; assessed competence; no risk scale used (NICE NG225).
Self-harm as emotional regulation vs suicidal intent; depression; bullying and identity stress as triggers; safeguarding concerns.
Asked directly about suicidal thoughts, plans, intent and means, and about protective factors.
Low mood with repeated self-harm and passive suicidal thoughts, no current plan, strong protective factors — stated without labelling her risk level.
Referral to young people’s mental health services with consent, co-produced safety plan, crisis numbers, school support she controls.
Online bullying addressed; sexuality handled without comment and kept confidential; sleep and phone use raised.
999, A&E and NHS 111 for crisis; Childline; wound safety-net; review in a week with time alone.

social.t: Online abuse follows a young person home and into the night. Ask about it directly, consider screen-time and sleep, and offer school involvement that she controls.
Fear of being outed is a strong driver of distress. Her sexuality is her private information; disclosure to parents is her choice alone.

legal.t: GMC 0–18 years: respect a competent young person’s confidentiality; disclose without consent only where necessary to protect them or others from risk of death or serious harm, and tell them first where possible.

Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech AHA (1985): a young person under 16 can consent if they have sufficient understanding and intelligence. Assess and record competence for decisions about confidentiality and referral.

If the online contact involves threats, sexual images or exploitation, this becomes a safeguarding concern requiring referral to children’s social care (and possibly CEOP/police), following local procedures.

professional.t: Never promise absolute secrecy. Explain the exception, document the confidentiality discussion, the direct risk questions and her answers, and the reasons for the decision not to share.
GMC 0–18 years supports seeing young people on their own for part of the consultation. Involve parents with the young person’s agreement, and in the words she chooses.

community.t: Childline (0800 1111), Papyrus HOPELINE for young people with suicidal thoughts, school pastoral or counselling support, local LGBT+ youth services, and locally commissioned online support for young people.

redFlags: Suicidal thoughts with a plan, intent, preparation or access to means — same-day crisis assessment
Escalating frequency or severity of self-harm; deep or infected wounds
Online threats, sexual images or exploitation — safeguarding referral
psychosocial: Online bullying; late-night phone use and poor sleep
Questioning her sexuality; fear of her parents’ reaction
Protective factors: younger sister, best friend, art
ice: Concern: everything will be told to her parents, including her sexuality
Expectation: to be told she’s fine so her mum backs off

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Low mood with repeated superficial self-cutting over about four months as a coping strategy, and passive suicidal thoughts without plan or intent, triggered by online bullying and fear about her sexuality. Strong protective factors. Competent to engage in decisions about her care.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “You’ve been carrying a lot on your own, and the cutting has become a way to let the pressure out. You’re low, and sometimes you feel others would be better off without you. That means you need more support — not that you’re in trouble.”

management.reflectIce: “You were worried I’d tell your mum everything. I won’t do anything behind your back, and who knows about the private parts is your choice.”
management.psychosocial: Co-produce what her mother is told; offer a single trusted contact at school for the bullying; respect her control over her sexuality; address sleep and phone use gently.
sharedPlan: Referral to children and young people’s mental health services for psychosocial assessment, with her consent (NICE NG225)
Written safety plan: triggers, what helps, people to contact, crisis numbers
Psychological therapy is first-line for low mood in young people (NICE NG134); no medication for self-harm
safetyNet: 999, A&E or NHS 111 for urgent mental health help if a plan develops or she cannot keep safe; Childline any time
Wound care advice; review in one week, seen alone for part of it

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is won or lost in the first minute. Without an honest confidentiality statement, Maya stays closed; without direct risk questions, the candidate cannot be safe; and one careless comment about her sexuality ends the consultation.

items.fail: Starting with questions about mood before explaining confidentiality.
items.why: “Does not establish a safe environment for disclosure.” Her “tell my mum I’m fine” is a test of whether this room is private.
items.fix: Open with what stays private and the one exception, in plain words.

items.fail: Avoiding the suicide question because she seems guarded, or asking only “you’re not going to do anything silly, are you?”
items.why: “Does not gather sufficient information to make a safe assessment.” Leading or vague questions get a “no”.
items.fix: Ask directly about thoughts, plans, intent and means, then about what keeps her safe.

items.fail: Summarising risk as “low” or scoring it on a scale.
items.why: NICE NG225 advises against risk tools and low/medium/high labels to predict suicide or allocate care.
items.fix: Describe what she told you, her protective factors, and the needs the plan must meet.

items.fail: Promising total secrecy to win her trust.
items.why: An absolute promise may have to be broken; GMC 0–18 years requires honesty about limits.
items.fix: “It stays between us unless I’m seriously worried about your safety — and I’d talk to you first.”

items.fail: Reacting to the sexuality disclosure with a comment, a question about certainty, or moving straight past it.
items.why: Editorialising or ignoring it both read as judgement; she withdraws.
items.fix: Thank her, say it is nothing to be ashamed of, and make clear she controls who knows.

items.fail: Ending with a referral and “see you soon”, with no crisis plan or agreed message for her mother.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting; and the mother waiting outside needs a plan both can live with.
items.fix: Co-produce a safety plan, give crisis numbers, book a review in a week, and agree the exact words for her mum.
